title: Aggregation: GROUP BY, FILTER, ROLLUP and GROUPING SETS
goal: By the end, you can fold many rows into one line per group, choose between WHERE, HAVING and FILTER for a condition, add subtotal and total lines with ROLLUP, and spot the join that makes a total count one payment twice.
opening:
Picture the end of June at a small company whose app records card payments. Every shop that takes cards through it is waiting for a statement: how many payments it took this half-year, and how much money. Harbor Hotel's statement says 3,835.00. The hotel's own records say 3,355.00. Nobody typed a wrong number, and the database showed no error.

The query behind the statement adds up each shop's payments and its refunds in one go. It's easy to trust a total the database worked out. A database never slips on arithmetic, so the fault must lie somewhere else. It doesn't. The database added exactly the rows it was handed, and it was handed one payment twice.

In "Joins, including semi and anti joins", we paired rows from two tables and saw that a join can repeat a row. In this lesson, we'll fold many rows into one line per shop, filter before and after that fold, and add subtotal lines. Then we'll catch the payment that was counted twice. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The `payments` table holds one row per card payment, and each row says which shop was paid. Eight shops use the app, and six of them have taken at least one payment. You ask for one line per shop with its number of payments: `SELECT merchant_id, count(*) FROM payments GROUP BY merchant_id`. How many lines come back?
options: 8: one per shop, with 0 for the two that took nothing
warmup.why: GROUP BY makes one pile, called a group, for each different shop number it finds in the rows it reads. This query reads `payments`, and a shop that took no payments has no row there to start a pile, so 6 lines come back. Nothing in `payments` mentions shops 6 and 8. To list all 8 with a 0, start from the table of shops, `merchants`, and attach the payments with a LEFT JOIN, as the third section does. One line would be right if the query had no GROUP BY at all.

sections.h: One line per shop: GROUP BY sorts rows into piles and folds each pile
sections.body:
Let's meet the data first. The course database belongs to a small company whose app records card payments. People pay for groceries, coffee, train rides and hotel rooms with a card, and each payment becomes one row in a table called `payments`. A table works like a spreadsheet: each row is one payment, and each column is one fact about it.

`payment_id` numbers the payment. `merchant_id` says which shop was paid (the database calls a shop a merchant, and a hotel or a bus company counts as one). `amount_minor` is the amount in cents, so 4250 means 42.50. `status` says whether the payment `succeeded`, `failed` or is still `pending`, and `created_at` says when it happened. A second table, `merchants`, holds one row per shop with its name and country. The data is small on purpose: 37 payments at 8 shops, from January to June 2026.

We ask the database questions in SQL, the language most databases understand, and each question is called a query. The database program is PostgreSQL 18, a free database that many companies run.

Now the question. The company wants each shop's total of succeeded payments. You could ask once per shop, keeping only that shop's rows with `WHERE merchant_id = 1`, then 2, and so on: eight trips to the database, and you'd need the list of shops first. Or you could fetch every payment into your own program and add them up there. With 37 rows that works. With a million payments, the large data set that later lessons use, you'd ship a million rows out of the database to work out 2,500 numbers, one per shop.

The database can do the adding where the data lives. It starts with an **aggregate function**: a function that takes many values and returns one. `count(*)` counts rows, `sum(amount_minor)` adds up a column, and `avg`, `min` and `max` give the average, the smallest and the largest. Used alone, an aggregate folds every row the query sees into a single row: many rows in, one row out.

```postgresql
course=# SELECT count(*), sum(amount_minor) FROM payments WHERE status = 'succeeded';
 count |  sum
-------+--------
    30 | 720455
(1 row)
```

SELECT lists what to show, FROM names the table, and WHERE keeps only the rows that pass a condition. So that's 30 succeeded payments, worth 7,204.55 in all. (psql is PostgreSQL's own window for typing queries. It shows `course=#` while it waits, and prints each answer as a small table.)

Picture a shoebox of paper receipts at the end of the day. To tell each shop what it took, you'd sort the receipts into one envelope per shop. Then you'd count the receipts in each envelope and write the total on the front. `GROUP BY merchant_id` does exactly that. Instead of one pile of rows, PostgreSQL makes one pile for each different `merchant_id`, called a **group**, and runs each aggregate on each pile separately. The column you group by is the group's key. Each group becomes one line of the answer. The envelope is the group, and the number on its front is the aggregate.

That's the picture for this whole lesson: **sort the rows into groups by a key, then fold each group into one row.** The stepper below runs it on the ten March payments.

The picture explains the rule that trips up everyone at first. After grouping, one line of the answer stands for a whole group. So a column may appear there only if it has one value per group: the column you grouped by, or an aggregate. `SELECT merchant_id, status, count(*) ... GROUP BY merchant_id` fails. Shop 2's group holds succeeded and failed payments, and PostgreSQL won't pick a status for you.

There's one exception, from the lesson "Designing a schema: normalization and constraints". A table's primary key is the column whose value names each row and is never repeated. When you group by it, you may show any other column of that table, because the key decides it. If `m` is the short name a query gives the `merchants` table, `GROUP BY m.merchant_id` lets you print `m.name`.

Two more things follow from the picture. A group exists only if at least one row has that key. Shops 6 and 8 took no payments, so they get no envelope and no line. And aggregates skip NULL, the database's marker for a value that's missing or unknown. `sum` and `avg` ignore NULLs, `count(col)` counts only the values that aren't NULL, and `sum` over no rows at all returns NULL, not 0.

So far, every row in a pile counts. Next, we'll throw some rows away before the sorting, and some piles away after it.

refs.title: PostgreSQL 18: The GROUP BY and HAVING clauses (table expressions)

aside.title: How does the database find each shop's pile?
aside.body: It has two ways, and both give the same answer. It can sort all the rows by shop, so each shop's payments sit next to each other, then walk down the sorted list and close an envelope each time the shop changes. Or it can keep a small table in memory with one entry per shop and add each payment to its shop's entry as the rows go past. That kind of table is a hash table, which finds an entry from its key in one step. EXPLAIN, the command that shows how PostgreSQL plans to run a query, calls the two ways GroupAggregate and HashAggregate. PostgreSQL picks whichever it expects to be cheaper.

sections.h: Filtering before and after the fold: WHERE and HAVING
sections.body:
Now the team that watches for fraud wants the shops with more than five succeeded payments. The obvious query fails:

```postgresql
course=# SELECT merchant_id, count(*) FROM payments WHERE count(*) > 5 GROUP BY merchant_id;
ERROR:  aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE
LINE 1: SELECT merchant_id, count(*) FROM payments WHERE count(*) > ...
                                                         ^
```

The error makes sense once you know the order PostgreSQL works in. You write a query starting with SELECT, but the database doesn't read it top to bottom. It goes through the parts in a fixed order, which the lesson "The relational model, keys and NULL" called the logical order. FROM picks the table, WHERE picks the rows, GROUP BY sorts them into piles and HAVING picks the piles. Then the select list (the columns after SELECT) decides what to show, ORDER BY sorts the answer and LIMIT cuts it short. WHERE is step 2. It looks at one row at a time, before any group exists, so there's nothing to count yet.

**HAVING** is the same kind of filter, one step later. It looks at the folded rows, one per group, and keeps the ones whose condition is true:

```sql
SELECT merchant_id, count(*) AS payments
FROM payments
WHERE status = 'succeeded'      -- rows: before grouping
GROUP BY merchant_id
HAVING count(*) > 5             -- groups: after folding
ORDER BY merchant_id;           -- merchants 1, 4 and 5
```

In the receipts picture, WHERE throws out the cancelled receipts before you sort, and HAVING sets aside the envelopes too thin to report. The last frame of the stepper above was a HAVING. One query can use both, and they do different jobs: WHERE decides which rows go into the piles, and HAVING decides which piles come out. A condition on single rows, like `status = 'succeeded'`, belongs in WHERE. Then PostgreSQL drops those rows before it spends any work sorting them.

The order explains a small annoyance, too. `AS volume` gives a column a short name, called an alias. HAVING runs before the select list, where that name is made, so `HAVING volume > 100000` fails with `column "volume" does not exist`. Repeat the aggregate instead: `HAVING sum(amount_minor) > 100000`. ORDER BY runs last, so it may use the alias, as the SQL standard allows. PostgreSQL also accepts an alias in GROUP BY. That's an extra of its own, which Oracle, another widely used database program, added only recently.

You can group by any expression, not only a column. Monthly totals group by the month a payment falls in. `date_trunc('month', created_at)` returns the first moment of that month, and `to_char(created_at, 'YYYY-MM')` returns the month as text, such as `2026-03`. Both read the time in the session's time zone. The session is your connection to the database, and in the course database its time zone is UTC, the world's reference clock (London's time in winter).

That choice moves money between months. A payment at 23:30 on 31 March, New York time, is 03:30 on 1 April in UTC, so a report in UTC counts it in April. Pick the time zone the business means on purpose, and write it into the query with `AT TIME ZONE` when it isn't the session's.

Up to now, every aggregate reads every row of its group. Next, we'll let two counts in the same line read different rows.

steps: Run the first query and read the error. Which step of the logical order is WHERE?
Run the HAVING version. Predict which shops pass before you run it.
Run the monthly query. Then change its HAVING to `HAVING volume > 100000` and run it again.

SELECT merchant_id, count(*) AS payments
FROM payments
WHERE status = 'succeeded'
GROUP BY merchant_id
HAVING count(*) > 5
ORDER BY merchant_id;

SELECT to_char(created_at, 'YYYY-MM') AS month, count(*) AS payments, sum(amount_minor) AS volume
FROM payments
WHERE status = 'succeeded'
GROUP BY month

---------+----------+--------

`GROUP BY month` works because PostgreSQL lets GROUP BY use a name made in the select list. `HAVING volume > 100000` fails with `ERROR:  column "volume" does not exist`, because HAVING runs before the select list.

sections.h: Two counts side by side: FILTER folds only the rows it names
sections.body:
The fraud team now wants one line per shop with its succeeded and failed counts side by side. `GROUP BY merchant_id, status` has the numbers, but stacked: one line per shop and status, so shop 2 takes two lines. The report wants them across, with one column per status. Turning values that sit in rows into columns is called **pivoting**.

Go back to the envelopes. Every aggregate in a grouped query reads the rows of its group. Give one aggregate a condition, and it reads only the rows that pass. It's like a second line on each envelope that counts only the declined receipts. SQL spells it `FILTER`:

```sql
SELECT merchant_id,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'succeeded') AS succeeded,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed')    AS failed,
       count(*)                                     AS total
FROM payments
GROUP BY merchant_id;
```

Each group is still read once. The three counts look at the same rows and keep different ones. PostgreSQL added FILTER in version 9.4, in 2014. Before that, and in databases without it, people write `sum(CASE WHEN status = 'failed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`. CASE gives 1 for a failed row and 0 for any other, and the sum adds them up, which comes to the same numbers.

FILTER and WHERE do different jobs. WHERE removes rows from every aggregate, and a group that loses all its rows disappears: `WHERE status = 'failed' GROUP BY merchant_id` returns only shops 2, 4 and 7. FILTER removes rows from one aggregate and keeps the group, so a shop with no failures stays in the report with a 0.

Rates bring two traps. `count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') * 100 / count(*)` divides whole numbers, and PostgreSQL then throws the fraction away, as most programming languages do. One failure in eight payments gives 12, not 12.5. Write `100.0 *` to make it a decimal number. And a shop with no payments puts 0 at the bottom of the fraction, which raises `division by zero`. `nullif(x, 0)` returns NULL when x is 0, and dividing by NULL gives NULL, which is the honest answer for "no payments".

The lab uses FILTER with a LEFT JOIN, from "Joins, including semi and anti joins". A join pairs each row of one table with the matching rows of another. A LEFT JOIN also keeps a row that found no match, and fills the other table's columns with NULL. So a shop with no payments gets one row, padded with NULLs. `count(*)` counts that row and says 1. Count a column from the payments side, `count(p.payment_id)`, and you get 0, because the padded row has NULL there.

One line per shop is right for a shop owner. The company's own report also wants a total per country and one grand total. Next, we'll add those lines without writing three queries.

In the second result, shop 4 shows `pct_int` 12 and `failed_pct` 12.5. Shop 2 shows 50 and 50.0, and shop 7 shows 25 and 25.0. Dividing whole numbers goes wrong only when the answer has a fraction, which is why tests with round numbers miss it.

sections.h: Subtotals and a grand total in one query: ROLLUP and GROUPING SETS
sections.body:
The company's report wants each shop's volume (the money it took), a subtotal per country and a grand total, all in one result. Each shop's country sits in the `merchants` table as a two-letter `country_code`, such as US or GB, so the query joins each payment to its shop. With what we have so far, that takes three queries glued together:

```sql
SELECT m.country_code, m.name, sum(p.amount_minor) FROM ... GROUP BY m.country_code, m.name
UNION ALL
SELECT m.country_code, NULL,   sum(p.amount_minor) FROM ... GROUP BY m.country_code
UNION ALL
SELECT NULL,           NULL,   sum(p.amount_minor) FROM ...;
```

`UNION ALL` stacks the rows of several queries that have the same columns, one under the other. It works, but you write the FROM and WHERE three times, and PostgreSQL reads the payments three times. Look at what differs between the three parts: only what we group by. SQL calls each way of grouping a **grouping set**, and lets you list several in one GROUP BY:

```sql
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((m.country_code, m.name), (m.country_code), ())
```

`()` is the empty grouping set: one group that holds every row, which gives the grand total. In the receipts picture, PostgreSQL sorts the same receipts three times: into envelopes per shop, into boxes per country, and into one big pile. Then it writes a total on each. A ladder like this one, where each set drops the last key of the one before, is so common that it has a short form: `ROLLUP (m.country_code, m.name)`.

Its sibling `CUBE (a, b)` makes every combination, `(a, b)`, `(a)`, `(b)` and `()`, for totals across and down a grid. Both arrived in PostgreSQL 9.5. The stepper shows ROLLUP adding its rows.

In a subtotal line, a column that isn't part of that set's key shows NULL. The subtotal for the US has NULL as its shop name, because it stands for all three US shops. That causes a real bug. If a key column can itself be NULL, say a payment that arrived with no channel, its ordinary group shows NULL there too, and the two lines look the same. `coalesce(channel, 'all')`, which swaps a NULL for 'all', labels both of them 'all'.

The function **GROUPING(col)** answers the real question. It returns 1 when `col` was rolled up in this line (folded away into a bigger group), and 0 when the line holds a real value there, NULL included. CASE then picks the label:

```sql
SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(m.name) = 1 THEN 'all merchants' ELSE m.name END AS merchant, ...
```

Sort with it as well. `ORDER BY GROUPING(m.country_code), m.country_code, GROUPING(m.name), m.name` puts each subtotal after its own lines and the grand total last, whatever the labels say.

So far, each payment has led to exactly one shop, and every total has been right. Next, we'll join a table where one payment can have several matches, and watch a total quietly grow.

sections.h: The payment counted twice: joining before you add up
sections.body:
Back to Harbor Hotel's statement from the opening. Each refund is a row in the `refunds` table, saying which payment it gives money back on and how much. A payment can have several refunds, so this link is one-to-many: one payment, many refunds. In database talk, the payment is the parent and its refunds are its children. Here's the query behind the statement. It shows each shop's payments together with their refunds:

```postgresql
course=# SELECT p.merchant_id, count(*) AS rows, sum(p.amount_minor) AS paid, sum(r.amount_minor) AS refunded
course-# FROM payments p
course-# LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.payment_id = p.payment_id
course-# WHERE p.status = 'succeeded'
course-# GROUP BY p.merchant_id ORDER BY p.merchant_id;
 merchant_id | rows |  paid  | refunded
-------------+------+--------+----------
           1 |    7 |  32934 |     3880
           2 |    3 |   5805 |        ∅
           3 |    4 |   1375 |        ∅
           4 |    7 | 340346 |   173899
           5 |    7 | 383500 |    18000
           7 |    3 |   4495 |        ∅
(6 rows)
```

(psql's `course-#` prompt means the query goes on from the line above, and ∅ marks a NULL: no refunds.) Harbor Hotel, shop 5, took six payments worth 3,355.00, yet the query says 3,835.00 from seven rows. FROM is step 1 of the logical order, so the join ran before the grouping. Payment 5 has two refunds, so the join made two rows for it, one beside each refund, and its 480.00 went into the hotel's pile twice.

GROUP BY folds whatever rows it's given. It can't know that two of them are the same payment. There's no error, and five of the six shops come out right, which is how this bug gets past a careful reader. In the receipts picture, it's two photocopies of one receipt in the envelope. A clerk would notice. GROUP BY never does.

**A join to many children repeats the parent once per child. Fold the children to one row each before you join.** A query in parentheses in FROM, given a name, acts like a table. (The next lesson, "Subqueries and common table expressions", covers these properly.)

```sql
SELECT p.merchant_id, sum(p.amount_minor) AS paid, coalesce(sum(r.refunded), 0) AS refunded
FROM payments p
LEFT JOIN (SELECT payment_id, sum(amount_minor) AS refunded
           FROM refunds
           GROUP BY payment_id) r ON r.payment_id = p.payment_id
WHERE p.status = 'succeeded'
GROUP BY p.merchant_id;
```

The inner query returns at most one row per payment, with its refunds already added up. So the join can no longer repeat a payment, and Harbor Hotel comes out at 3,355.00.

The tempting shortcut is `sum(DISTINCT p.amount_minor)`, which adds each different amount once. It fixes Harbor Hotel by luck and breaks two other shops. Metro Transit's rides cost 2.75, 2.75, 2.75 and 5.50, so the distinct sum is 8.25 instead of 13.75. Volt Electronics loses two of its three 189.99 payments. DISTINCT works on values, and two real payments can have the same value. For counting, `count(DISTINCT p.payment_id)` is safe, because every payment's number is unique. Sums need the folding first. When you see DISTINCT in a report's query, ask which duplicate it's hiding.

That's also where today's tools stop. Every one of them folds rows away: once an envelope is sealed, its receipts are gone from the answer. A question that compares each payment with something worked out from other payments, such as their average, needs more than a sealed envelope. The next lesson starts there.

steps: Run the first query. It's the one from this section, plus `sum(DISTINCT ...)`. Compare `paid` and `paid_distinct` for shops 3, 4 and 5.
Run the second query, which folds the refunds first. Which shop's `payments` count differs from its `rows` in the first query?

       sum(p.amount_minor) AS paid, sum(DISTINCT p.amount_minor) AS paid_distinct
FROM payments p
LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.payment_id = p.payment_id
WHERE p.status = 'succeeded'
GROUP BY p.merchant_id
ORDER BY p.merchant_id;

       coalesce(sum(r.refunded), 0) AS refunded
FROM payments p
LEFT JOIN (SELECT payment_id, sum(amount_minor) AS refunded
           FROM refunds GROUP BY payment_id) r ON r.payment_id = p.payment_id
WHERE p.status = 'succeeded'
GROUP BY p.merchant_id
ORDER BY p.merchant_id;

The first query shows the two wrong answers next to each other. Shop 5 has `paid` 383500 (payment 5 counted twice) and `paid_distinct` 335500 (right by luck), shop 3 has 1375 and 825, and shop 4 has 340346 and 302348. The second query is right for every shop:

```postgresql

-------------+----------+--------+----------
           1 |        7 |  32934 |     3880
           2 |        3 |   5805 |        0
           3 |        4 |   1375 |        0
           4 |        7 | 340346 |   173899
           5 |        6 | 335500 |    18000
           7 |        3 |   4495 |        0
(6 rows)
```

Shop 5 now has 6 rows instead of 7: one row per payment, as GROUP BY needs.

compare.title: Statuses as columns: Oracle PIVOT and PostgreSQL FILTER

a.label: Oracle
a.title: Oracle (11g and later)
a.src:
-- PIVOT groups by every input column it does not use
SELECT *
FROM (SELECT merchant_id, status, payment_id FROM payments)
PIVOT (count(payment_id) FOR status IN ('succeeded' AS succeeded,
                                        'failed'    AS failed,
                                        'pending'   AS pending))
ORDER BY merchant_id;

-- portable form, in older code everywhere:
--   sum(CASE WHEN status = 'failed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

b.label: PostgreSQL 18
b.title: PostgreSQL 18
b.src:
-- no PIVOT: one FILTER per output column
SELECT merchant_id,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'succeeded') AS succeeded,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed')    AS failed,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'pending')   AS pending
FROM payments
GROUP BY merchant_id
ORDER BY merchant_id;

-- the tablefunc extension's crosstab() also pivots,
-- but FILTER is plain SQL and easier to read

compare.note: Oracle is another database program, sold by the company of the same name and run by many large firms. Both queries return one line per shop with a column per status. Oracle's `PIVOT` groups by every column of its input that it neither counts nor turns into a column, without saying so. An extra column in the inner query (say `created_at`) quietly turns the result into one line per payment, which is why the input is a narrow subquery. PostgreSQL has no PIVOT, and FILTER keeps the grouping in plain sight in GROUP BY. Oracle's newest release, Oracle AI Database 26ai, also accepts the standard `FILTER` clause and a GROUP BY that uses names from the select list, so the PostgreSQL form works there too. `ROLLUP`, `CUBE`, `GROUPING SETS` and `GROUPING()` are the same in both, and Oracle's `GROUPING_ID(a, b)` does what PostgreSQL's `GROUPING(a, b)` does with several columns.

worked.title: A monthly statement for Volt Electronics, without counting anything twice

steps.say: Volt Electronics (shop 4) wants a statement: for each month, the succeeded payments it took, the refunds it gave and what's left (the net), plus a total line. A refund counts in the month it was given. Joining payments to refunds would pair rows and risk the repeat from the last section, so stack the two kinds of money movement into one list instead. `UNION ALL` puts one query's rows under the other's, and pairs nothing.
steps.code:
-- 1. one row per money movement, tagged with its kind
SELECT to_char(p.created_at, 'YYYY-MM') AS month, 'payment' AS kind, p.amount_minor
FROM payments p
WHERE p.merchant_id = 4 AND p.status = 'succeeded'
UNION ALL
SELECT to_char(r.created_at, 'YYYY-MM'), 'refund', r.amount_minor
FROM refunds r
JOIN payments p ON p.payment_id = r.payment_id   -- one payment per refund: no repeat
WHERE p.merchant_id = 4;
-- 10 rows: 7 payments and 3 refunds

steps.say: Group the movements by month and split the fold with FILTER: one sum for payments, one for refunds. Wrap each sum in `coalesce(..., 0)`, because in a month with no refunds the refund sum adds up no rows, and that gives NULL.
steps.code:
-- 2. fold per month; each sum reads only its own kind
SELECT month,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'payment')                       AS payments,
       coalesce(sum(amount_minor) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'payment'), 0) AS gross,
       coalesce(sum(amount_minor) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'refund'), 0)  AS refunds
FROM ( /* the UNION ALL from step 1 */ ) AS movements
GROUP BY month;

steps.say: Add the total line with `ROLLUP (month)`, which is short for `GROUPING SETS ((month), ())`. Label that line with GROUPING, and sort it last with GROUPING too.
steps.code:
-- 3. the statement
SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(month) = 1 THEN 'total' ELSE month END AS month,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'payment')                         AS payments,
       coalesce(sum(amount_minor) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'payment'), 0)   AS gross,
       coalesce(sum(amount_minor) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'refund'), 0)    AS refunds,
       coalesce(sum(amount_minor) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'payment'), 0)
     - coalesce(sum(amount_minor) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'refund'), 0)    AS net
FROM ( /* the UNION ALL from step 1 */ ) AS movements
GROUP BY ROLLUP (month)
ORDER BY GROUPING(month), month;

steps.say: Check the result against what you already know. The gross total, 340,346 cents, matches Volt's `paid` in the last Try it, and the refunds, 173,899, match its `refunded`. March shows the three 189.99 payments, including the duplicate, payment 18, and the refund of 18 the next day. January nets to 0, because payment 3 was refunded in full as fraud.

drill.title: Write a grouped report from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write one query over `payments` that gives, for each shop, the number of succeeded payments, their total amount and the number of failed payments. Keep only shops with at least one failure, and add a grand total line whose shop column says 'all'. Then say what would go wrong if you used WHERE instead of FILTER for the failed count.

answer.src:
SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(merchant_id) = 1 THEN 'all' ELSE merchant_id::text END AS merchant,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'succeeded')          AS succeeded,
       sum(amount_minor) FILTER (WHERE status = 'succeeded') AS volume,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed')             AS failed
FROM payments
GROUP BY ROLLUP (merchant_id)
HAVING count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') > 0     -- groups, after folding
ORDER BY GROUPING(merchant_id), merchant_id;
-- merchants 2, 4 and 7, then 'all' with 30 succeeded, 720455 and 5 failed.
-- WHERE status = 'failed' would remove the succeeded rows from every aggregate,
-- so succeeded and volume would come out as 0 and NULL.

recap: GROUP BY sorts rows into one group per key and folds each group into one line. The answer may show only the grouping key, aggregates, and columns that a grouped primary key decides.
WHERE filters single rows before the grouping, and HAVING filters the folded groups after it. Neither can see a name made in the select list.
`agg(...) FILTER (WHERE ...)` folds only some rows of each group, which turns values into columns in one pass. Watch whole-number division, and divide by `nullif(x, 0)`.
`ROLLUP (a, b)` is `GROUPING SETS ((a, b), (a), ())`, and CUBE gives every combination. GROUPING(col) tells a subtotal's NULL from a real NULL.
A join to many children repeats the parent once per child, so fold each child table to one row per key before joining. `sum(DISTINCT ...)` is not a fix.
The limit: every tool here folds rows away. Once a group is one line, its payments are gone from the answer, so comparing each payment with its shop's average needs more than GROUP BY.
closing:
We started with Harbor Hotel's statement, 480.00 too high. The database added exactly what the join handed it: payment 5 twice, once beside each of its refunds. Folding the refunds first fixed it, and DISTINCT would only have hidden it.

To see the copies yourself, run this in psql: `SELECT p.payment_id, r.refund_id FROM payments p LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.payment_id = p.payment_id WHERE p.merchant_id = 5;`. Payment 5 shows up on two lines before any adding happens. Next time an app shows you a total, ask what one row stood for before it was added up.

Next, we'll answer two-step questions, such as which payments are larger than the average, by putting one query inside another.

quiz.q: `SELECT country_code, count(*) FROM merchants WHERE count(*) > 1 GROUP BY country_code` should list the countries with more than one shop, and it fails. What's the fix?
options: Write `WHERE count > 1`, using the column's name
quiz.why: WHERE runs on single rows, before any group exists, so it can't use an aggregate. HAVING runs on the folded rows, one per country, where the count exists. An aggregate can't go in GROUP BY either, and `count` in WHERE isn't a column at all, so the third option fails with a different error.

quiz.q: Shops 2, 4 and 7 have failed payments, and 6 shops have payments in all. How many lines does `SELECT merchant_id, count(*) FROM payments WHERE status = 'failed' GROUP BY merchant_id` return?
options: 6, with 0 for the shops without failures
quiz.why: WHERE removes the other rows before the grouping, so only shops 2, 4 and 7 have rows to start a group. The tempting 6 is what you'd get with the condition on the aggregate instead: `count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed')` keeps all six shops and shows 0 for the ones without failures.

quiz.q: A shop's order has 3 lines (one per item) and 2 shipments (one per parcel). A report joins `orders o JOIN order_lines l ON ... JOIN shipments s ON ...` and then adds up `sum(l.quantity)` per order. How many times is each line's quantity added?
options: It depends on how PostgreSQL chooses to run the join
quiz.why: The join pairs every line with every shipment of the same order: 3 times 2 is 6 rows, so each line appears twice. How PostgreSQL runs a join never changes which rows come out, so the last option is out. Fold the lines and the shipments to one row per order each, then join.

quiz.q: A report groups customers with `ROLLUP (region)` and labels the total line with `coalesce(region, 'Total')`. Some customers have no region, so theirs is NULL. What does the output show?
options: Two lines labelled Total, one of them only the customers with no region
One Total line, because ROLLUP merges the NULL group into it
An error, because ROLLUP doesn't allow NULL keys
The NULL group is left out
quiz.why: The customers with no region form an ordinary group whose key is NULL, and the grand total line also has NULL there. coalesce can't tell them apart, so both get the label. `CASE WHEN GROUPING(region) = 1 THEN 'Total' ELSE region END` can, because GROUPING is 1 only on the rolled-up line.

quiz.q: `merchants m LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id ... GROUP BY m.merchant_id`. Paper Lantern Books took no payments. What do `count(*)` and `count(p.payment_id)` return for it?
quiz.why: A LEFT JOIN, from Joins, including semi and anti joins, keeps a shop that found no payment as one row, with NULL in every payments column. `count(*)` counts rows, so it says 1. `count(p.payment_id)` counts the values that aren't NULL, so it says 0, which is the answer you want.

flashcards.front: What may appear in the answer of a grouped query?
flashcards.back: The grouping keys, aggregates, and columns of a table whose primary key you grouped by (the key decides them).

flashcards.front: WHERE or HAVING: which runs first, and on what?
flashcards.back: WHERE, on single rows, before the grouping. HAVING runs after the fold, on one row per group.
Only the rows of the group that pass the condition. Other aggregates in the same query still see every row.

flashcards.front: `ROLLUP (a, b)` is short for which grouping sets?
flashcards.back: `GROUPING SETS ((a, b), (a), ())`. `CUBE (a, b)` adds `(b)` as well.

flashcards.front: How do you tell a subtotal line from a group whose key is NULL?
flashcards.back: `GROUPING(col)` is 1 when col was rolled up on that line, and 0 for a real value, NULL included.

flashcards.front: Why does `sum(p.amount_minor)` grow after joining payments to refunds?
flashcards.back: The join repeats a payment once per refund, and GROUP BY folds every copy. Fold the refunds per payment first.

flashcards.front: What does `sum(x)` return over zero rows?
flashcards.back: NULL, not 0. Wrap it in `coalesce(sum(x), 0)` when 0 is the right answer.

terms.plain: A function that folds many values into one: count, sum, avg, min, max.
All the rows that share the same GROUP BY values. Each group becomes one line of the answer.
A filter on the folded groups. It runs after GROUP BY and before the select list.
`agg(...) FILTER (WHERE cond)`: the aggregate reads only the rows of its group that pass cond.
Turning values that sit in rows (one row per status) into columns (one column per status).
One list of columns to group by. GROUPING SETS runs several of them over the same rows in one query.
Short forms for grouping sets. ROLLUP drops keys from the right to make subtotals; CUBE uses every combination.
Returns 1 for a column that was rolled up on this line, and 0 where the line holds a real value.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate's half-year report showed higher totals for some shops after they added a LEFT JOIN to refunds, so they changed `sum(p.amount_minor)` to `sum(DISTINCT p.amount_minor)`. Now other shops come out too low. Explain both bugs and the fix.
explain_back.answer: The join runs before the grouping, and it makes one row for every refund a payment has. So a payment with two refunds lands in its shop's group twice, and its amount is added twice. GROUP BY can't tell that two rows are one payment. `sum(DISTINCT ...)` adds each different amount once, so two real payments with the same amount, like three 2.75 bus rides, collapse into one, and those shops come out low. DISTINCT works on values, not on which payment a row is. The fix is to fold the refunds to one row per payment first, `SELECT payment_id, sum(amount_minor) FROM refunds GROUP BY payment_id`, and LEFT JOIN that, so each payment appears once. Stacking payments and refunds with UNION ALL and grouping once also works.

deeper.body:
How much does ROLLUP save over three GROUP BY queries stacked with UNION ALL? Try it on the large data set: a million made-up payments at 2,500 shops, in the same tables under a separate schema (a named folder of tables) called `big`. Load it once with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course -f /seed/load-big.sql`, then type `SET search_path = big, public;` in psql. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)` runs a query and prints the plan PostgreSQL followed, with real times. The ROLLUP plan reads the million payments once and fills three hash tables at the same time:

```postgresql
course=# EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF)
course-# SELECT status, metadata->>'channel' AS channel, count(*), sum(amount_minor)
course-# FROM payments GROUP BY ROLLUP (status, metadata->>'channel');
                                   QUERY PLAN
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 MixedAggregate (actual time=309.529..309.550 rows=16.00 loops=1)
   Hash Key: status, (metadata ->> 'channel'::text)
   Hash Key: status
   Group Key: ()
   Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 105kB
   Buffers: shared hit=977 read=22841
   ->  Seq Scan on payments (actual time=0.291..129.376 rows=1000478.00 loops=1)
(output trimmed)
 Execution Time: 309.694 ms
```

Each `Hash Key` line is one grouping set, and `Group Key: ()` is the grand total. Buffers are the table's 8 kB pages, read from memory (`hit`) or from disk (`read`). The UNION ALL version reads the table three times: 71,480 buffers against 23,818. On an Apple-silicon laptop it still finished first, in about 250 ms against 310 ms. PostgreSQL ran its three parts in parallel workers, helper processes that each read part of the table at once, and it doesn't run grouping sets in parallel. So ROLLUP reads less and is one statement to maintain, and whether it's faster depends on how many cores sit idle. Your times will differ with the machine.

Aggregates can build things other than numbers. `string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY name)` joins strings, `array_agg(payment_id ORDER BY created_at)` builds a list, and `bool_and(status = 'succeeded')` asks whether every row passed. The `ORDER BY` inside the parentheses orders the values fed to that one aggregate. It's the only way to get a set order inside `string_agg`, because a group, like a table, has no order of its own.

`count(DISTINCT x)` has to remember every different value it has seen in the group, so on large groups it sorts, and it's much slower than `count(*)`. If you need an exact distinct count often, consider a table that keeps one row per (group, value) pair, so the count becomes a plain `count(*)`.
